name: Iron
summary: Iron is a mineral the body needs to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The body has no active way to get rid of extra iron, so it controls how much it absorbs: too little leads to anaemia, and too much builds up and can damage organs.
roles: Carrying oxygen in the blood (haemoglobin) and in muscles (myoglobin)
Normal brain development in babies and children

status.note: Ferritin is the usual test for iron stores: a low ferritin means stores are low. But ferritin also rises with inflammation, infection, liver disease and excess body fat, so a normal or high ferritin can hide low iron when CRP (C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation) is raised. Transferrin saturation (how much of the iron-carrying protein in blood is loaded with iron) helps here: low in iron deficiency, high in iron overload. Serum iron on its own changes a lot through the day and after meals, so it says little by itself. Haemoglobin, MCV (mean cell volume, the size of red cells) and MCH (mean cell haemoglobin) fall only late, once deficiency has become anaemia.

signs: Shortness of breath on effort, a fast heartbeat
Brittle nails, hair loss, a sore tongue or cracks at the corners of the mouth
Often no symptoms at all when stores are low but anaemia hasn't developed yet
atRisk: Women with periods, especially heavy periods
Babies, young children and teenagers, who grow fast
People who lose blood from the gut (e.g. ulcers, bowel polyps or cancer), often without noticing
People with coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or after weight-loss (bariatric) surgery
Vegetarians and vegans, because iron from plants is absorbed less well
People with heart failure or chronic kidney disease
Long-term use of acid-reducing medicines or regular use of anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) or aspirin

signs: From supplements: constipation, diarrhoea, nausea, stomach pain and black stools
Long-term overload: tiredness, joint pain, loss of sex drive, darker skin
Long-term overload: liver damage (scarring, cirrhosis), diabetes and heart problems
Overdose (mostly young children swallowing tablets): vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach pain, then shock and liver failure
high.note: With a normal gut, food alone almost never causes iron overload, because the body absorbs less when stores are full. Overload usually comes from inherited haemochromatosis (the body absorbs too much iron), repeated blood transfusions (e.g. thalassaemia), or iron supplements taken without a deficiency over a long time. Haemochromatosis shows up as a high transferrin saturation and a high ferritin, and is treated by a doctor by removing blood. A high ferritin on its own far more often reflects inflammation, fatty liver or alcohol than too much iron. An overdose of iron tablets is a medical emergency, especially in young children.

examples: Red meat and liver (liver is high in vitamin A, so it isn't advised in pregnancy)
Dark poultry meat, fish and shellfish such as mussels and cockles
Fortified breakfast cereals and wholemeal bread
Pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, nuts and dried apricots
Dark green leafy vegetables such as kale
foodSources.note: Iron from meat and fish (haem iron) is absorbed much better than iron from plants and supplements (non-haem iron). Vitamin C in the same meal helps the body absorb plant iron. Tea, coffee and cocoa with a meal, and calcium, reduce it. Phytate in whole grains and pulses also lowers absorption.

forms.name: Ferrous salts (ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate)
forms.note: The standard, cheapest forms, used in most trials. They contain different amounts of iron per tablet, so labels that give the weight of the salt and labels that give the amount of elemental (actual) iron aren't comparable. Stomach and gut side effects are common.

forms.name: Ferrous bisglycinate (an iron-amino acid chelate)
forms.note: Iron bound to the amino acid glycine. In trials in pregnant women it raised haemoglobin a little more and caused fewer gut side effects than iron salts, but there are few trials in other adults (see the findings below).

forms.name: Ferric forms (ferric maltol, polysaccharide-iron complex, others)
forms.note: Most ferric (Fe3+) iron is absorbed less well than ferrous (Fe2+) iron. Ferric maltol is a prescription medicine designed to be absorbed better; other ferric products have less research behind them.

forms.name: Slow-release and coated tablets
forms.note: These release iron further down the gut, past the first part of the small intestine where most iron is absorbed. They may cause fewer side effects partly because less iron is taken up.

forms.name: Liquid iron
forms.note: Easier to swallow and to give in small amounts; it can stain teeth.

forms.name: Intravenous iron (a drip)
forms.note: A medicine given in a clinic, not a supplement. Used when tablets don't work, can't be absorbed (e.g. some bowel diseases) or aren't tolerated, or when iron is needed quickly.

forms.name: Daily or every other day, once or split
forms.note: Each iron dose raises hepcidin, a hormone that blocks iron absorption for about a day. In absorption studies, single doses on alternate days were absorbed better per dose than daily or split doses. Whether this gives better haemoglobin over months is still unclear (see the findings below).

reference.noUpperLimit: EFSA could not set a tolerable upper intake level for iron (2024): it is clear that iron overload damages organs, but the studies don't show at what intake the risk starts. Instead it set a "safe level of intake" of 40 mg a day from all sources for adults, including in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It is based on supplement trials where 20–25 mg a day on top of about 15 mg from food did not cause black stools (a sign of unabsorbed iron in the gut, not harmful in itself). This is more cautious, and more limited, than an upper limit: it says what is safe, not where harm begins. Doctors treating iron deficiency often use higher amounts for a limited time. The pregnancy value equals the value for women before menopause because absorption rises sharply in pregnancy.

interactions.note: Iron binds levothyroxine in the gut, so less of the medicine is absorbed. The two are usually taken several hours apart; a pharmacist or doctor can advise on timing.

interactions.with: Some antibiotics (tetracyclines such as doxycycline, and quinolones such as ciprofloxacin)
interactions.note: Iron binds these antibiotics, so both are absorbed less. Timing matters; ask a pharmacist.

interactions.with: Levodopa and some other medicines (e.g. methyldopa, bisphosphonates for bones)
interactions.note: Iron can reduce how much of these medicines is absorbed.

interactions.with: Acid-reducing medicines (proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, H2 blockers, antacids)
interactions.note: Stomach acid helps absorb non-haem iron, so long-term use of these medicines can lower iron absorption and iron stores.
Calcium reduces iron absorption from the same meal or tablet. Over a whole diet the effect on iron stores appears small.
High doses of iron and zinc taken together without food compete for absorption.
Polyphenols in these drinks strongly reduce iron absorption from the same meal.

interactions.with: Haemochromatosis, thalassaemia and other iron-loading conditions
interactions.note: Iron supplements (and vitamin C supplements, which increase iron absorption) can add to iron overload. People with these conditions are guided by their doctor.
Iron tablets can worsen gut symptoms and are absorbed less during inflammation; doctors often use iron by drip instead.

Iron needs rise in the second half of pregnancy, and anaemia is checked in antenatal care. EFSA's safe level of 40 mg a day also applies in pregnancy. Iron in pregnancy is decided with a midwife or doctor.

cautions: An overdose of iron tablets can kill a young child. Keep them out of sight and reach; a swallowed overdose needs emergency care.
Low iron has a cause, and in men and in women after menopause it can be blood loss from the gut that needs checking. A doctor finds the cause before treating it.

Iron supplements without a confirmed deficiency can be harmful, especially with haemochromatosis. The gene change behind it is common in people of northern European descent, and many people with the condition don't know they have it.
A high ferritin is usually a sign of inflammation, liver strain or alcohol, not a need for less iron in the diet; it is worth discussing with a doctor.

commonUses: May treat or prevent iron-deficiency anaemia
May reduce tiredness when iron is low

origin: Iron is a mineral that comes from food: meat, fish and shellfish (haem iron, absorbed well) and plants, fortified foods and supplements (non-haem iron, absorbed less). The body recycles most of its iron and has no active way to get rid of extra.
Supplement iron is a manufactured salt or chelate, such as ferrous sulfate or ferrous bisglycinate, sometimes given by drip in medical care.
dosage: EFSA's reference intake is 11 mg a day for men and for women after menopause, and 16 mg for women before menopause and in pregnancy. These are population values for the whole diet, not personal targets.
Iron supplements are best checked against a blood test first, and the safety information below explains why. Check the iron content in mg on the label, and do not add several products together.

targets.label: EFSA reference intake, men and women after menopause
EFSA reference intake, women before menopause

foods.name: Lamb liver, raw
foods.note: Liver is very high in vitamin A, so it is not advised in pregnancy.

foods.name: Lean raw beef (mince to rump steak)
foods.note: Haem iron, absorbed better than plant iron.

foods.name: Lentils, boiled
foods.note: Non-haem iron. Vitamin C in the same meal helps absorption; tea and coffee reduce it.

foodAmounts.verdict: Yes, for the reference intake: ordinary meals with meat, fish, pulses, seeds and fortified cereals can reach 11–16 mg a day, and the table shows how much of single foods that is. These are amounts eaten, not absorbed, and plant iron is absorbed much less than meat iron. If iron stores are already low (heavy periods, pregnancy, a vegetarian diet), the amounts used to correct them are higher than the reference intake, so food alone and a supplement are different situations.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the raw or boiled food named. Other foods, brands and fortified products differ.
